subject: Cloud Computing
title: The Thundering Herd Problem
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Thundering Herd Problem.

hook.text: A cache server restarts. All 10,000 clients notice it's empty and hit the database simultaneously. The database crashes.

buildup.text: A thundering herd occurs when many processes react to the same event at the same time, overwhelming a shared resource.

discovery.text: The fix: stagger requests with jitter, use cache warming, and implement request coalescing — one fetch for many waiters.

twist.text: Thundering herds often happen during recovery from another failure. The system breaks twice: outage, then stampede.

climax.text: Designing for recovery is as important as designing for normal operation. How your system wakes up matters.

punchline.text: The recovery was worse than the outage. Plan for the stampede.

quiz.question: What causes a thundering herd problem?
options: Many clients reacting to the same event simultaneously and overwhelming a shared resource
A single user making too many requests per second
Cloud providers limiting the number of active connections

details.summary: The thundering herd occurs when many clients simultaneously reconnect after an outage, overwhelming the recovering service with a surge of requests that causes it to fail again. This pattern turns brief outages into prolonged cascading failures.
details.whyItMatters: Without backoff and jitter in client retry logic, recovering services face demand spikes many times normal load. The thundering herd turns every brief outage into a potential extended one.
takeaways: Mass simultaneous reconnections overwhelm recovering services
Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retry load over time
Circuit breakers prevent clients from overwhelming servers

faq.question: What causes the thundering herd?
faq.answer: When a service goes down, all connected clients start retrying simultaneously. When the service comes back, it faces a concentrated burst of requests many times greater than normal traffic. Without staggered retries, the burst can crash the service again repeatedly.

faq.question: How is the thundering herd prevented?
faq.answer: Implement exponential backoff with random jitter in all client retry logic so retries spread over time. Use circuit breakers that stop retrying after repeated failures. Gradually ramp up capacity during recovery rather than accepting all traffic at once.
